title: He won the war.
paragraphs: But almost lost his soul right after.
Because that’s where most people fall.

Not in the battle…
—but in the blessing.
Abram just came back from blood, dust, and chaos.

Victory clung to his skin.
Sweat still traced his muscles.
The sound of clashing swords still echoed in his memory.
He had every reason to feel powerful.

Every reason to say,
“I did this.”
But before pride could crown him…

Out of nowhere.
No introduction.
No backstory.
And a blessing that would shatter Abram’s ego before it could grow.
Here’s the tension you can’t ignore:
Why would God interrupt a victory moment?
Why not let him feel strong?
Because God knows something we keep forgetting:
Victory is the most dangerous place for your soul.
Because failure makes you cry out to God.
But victory tempts you to replace Him.
You didn’t fall when life was hard.
You prayed more when you were desperate.
You sought God when everything was breaking.
That’s when something subtle crept in.

“You handled that.”
“You survived that.”
“You built this.”
And suddenly, the God who carried you…
…gets reduced to a background character in your own story.

“Then Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine.
He was priest of God Most High.
And he blessed Abram, saying,
‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High,
Possessor of heaven and earth;
and blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your enemies into your hand!’”
— Genesis 14:18–20
Because some of you are living in victories you secretly took credit for.
But forgot the nights God held your mind together.
But forgot the grace that kept you from collapsing.
But you forgot who carried you when you were weak.
And here comes the deeper mystery.
Some scholars interpret him as a historical king-priest.
Others see him as a foreshadowing—a type pointing forward.
Because hundreds of years later, Scripture pulls back the curtain:

Jesus Christ is called
“a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” (Hebrews 7)
Because one day, another Priest would come.
Not with bread and wine as symbols only…
This isn’t just about ancient kings.
Your silent belief that you’re “doing okay now.”
That’s the most dangerous lie you will ever believe.
You can pray and still be proud.
You can serve and still be self-centered.
You can talk about God and still sit on the throne of your own life.
But the Gospel doesn’t negotiate with pride.
Because the cross says something offensive:
You were not strong enough to save yourself.
And no amount of discipline, effort, or self-improvement could fix that.
To replace what you could never be.

Your sin was exposed.
Your pride was crushed.
Your self-reliance was dismantled.
He doesn’t just remind you who gave the victory—
He doesn’t just point you to God—
And here’s the truth that will set you free:
You don’t have to pretend anymore.
You don’t have to act strong.
You don’t have to carry your image.
You don’t have to protect your pride.
Because everything you’re trying to build your identity on…
So what do you do with this?
Because when grace hits your heart—
You stop gripping your life like it’s yours.
Not when you feel more ready.
What victory are you secretly taking credit for?

What area of your life are you saying, “I did this,”
when deep down you know God carried you?
What pride have you baptized with spiritual language?
What sin are you managing instead of surrendering?
Jesus is not exposing you to shame you.
He’s exposing you to free you.

The pride.
The performance.
The illusion of control.
Because the same God who delivered Abram…
The same Christ who conquered sin and death…
Let this be the moment you stop worshiping your survival…
You’ll need to come back to this truth.
